targets.approach: No trail reaches Rimrock Ridge. The way in is the north end of the Ptarmigan Traverse. Start at the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of the Cascade River Road and climb the Cascade Pass trail, then follow the traverse's climbers' path over Cache Col and down to Kool-Aid Lake, the usual first camp. The next day crosses the exposed Red Ledge below Arts Knoll and the crevassed Middle Cascade Glacier (rope up) to the Spider–Formidable col, then drops to Yang Yang Lakes, the usual second camp. On the third day the traverse climbs back to the Le Conte ridge and up the Le Conte Glacier to the col between Le Conte and Sentinel at its head. The parties on record left the traverse here, passed north of Sentinel Peak and followed the ridge east along its crest; the ridge is the divide between Flat Creek and the West Fork of Agnes Creek. Beyond the traverse the line is cross-country alpine ground with no path, and no detailed description of it is published. The Agnes Creek trail (PCT) from High Bridge runs up a different valley and does not lead to the ridge.
targets.descent_text: Retrace the ridge crest, downclimbing the rock steps and bypassing towers on the same side used on ascent.

targets.approach: South Face is another wall within the same Squire Creek Walls complex as Waterfall Basin, reached from the same Darrington trailhead: I-5 to the Arlington exit, SR 530 east through Oso to Darrington, then Squire Creek Road to the washout-blocked parking area. From there, walk the old roadbed past the flagged landslide crossing to the Squire Creek Trail sign and on to two cut logs with old logging cable, turn right onto the boot track, ford Squire Creek, and climb steeply through old-growth forest up two gullies to the grassy saddle below the South Face, roughly 3 hours from the car. For Doorway Flake, go west along the base of the wall past the start of Skeena26 and scramble 4th class onto the far western wall.
targets.descent_text: Rappel the line of ascent using the fixed hand-drilled bolt and Fixe chain anchors; two 60m ropes recommended.

targets.approach: South Face is another wall within the same Squire Creek Walls complex as Waterfall Basin, reached via the same Darrington-area approach: I-5 to the Arlington exit, SR 530 east through Oso to Darrington, then Squire Creek Road to the washout-blocked parking area. From there, follow the rough, unmaintained climbers' approach — the old roadbed past a landslide crossing to a boot track that drops to a ford of Squire Creek, then a climbers' track across a tributary and up through old-growth forest into two steep, dirty gullies that top out on the grassy saddle below the South Face, roughly 3 hours from the car, with route-finding (flagging, cairns) required in several spots.
targets.descent_text: Rappel the line of ascent; 50-meter ropes are adequate for most pitches, while 60-meter ropes allow combining pitches 5 and 6 to speed the descent.

targets.approach: South Face is the southwest-facing slab wall around the corner west of the Illusion Wall, with its own approach separate from Waterfall Basin. Take I-5 to the Arlington exit, SR 530 east through Oso to Darrington, then Squire Creek Road to the washout-blocked parking area. Walk the old roadbed past the flagged landslide crossing to the brown Squire Creek Trail #654 sign and 8-10 minutes beyond it, to two cut logs either side of the road with old logging cable visible. Turn right a few steps past them on a well-beaten boot track, drop to Squire Creek and ford it where it is shallowest (hard in early season or after storms), then follow the climbers' track briefly downstream before it turns uphill, crosses a tributary and climbs old-growth forest and two gullies, steep and dirty near the top, to the grassy saddle, about 3 hours from the car. For this route go left (west) from the saddle to the base of Skeena26, scramble about 100 m of class 4 ramps and small dihedrals to a large shelf, follow it left to a deep gully (two-bolt anchor for a hand line or a short rappel), cross it and follow a cairned boot track west across talus and cedar ribs to the large talus field below the far western wall, about an hour from Skeena26.
targets.descent_text: Descend by rappelling the line of ascent using the fixed hand-drilled bolt anchors; two 60m ropes recommended.

targets.approach: The genuine standard approach is from the Downey Creek Trailhead (off Suiattle River Road) via the southern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse — a rugged, largely off-trail alpine route over Itswoot Ridge/Cub Lake and Bachelor Creek involving glacier travel and significant bushwhacking. Climbers typically budget a full day (or two) of approach before reaching the base of South Peak's granite faces; this is an experienced-mountaineers-only objective, not a roadside crag.

targets.approach: When below the east face, scramble up through brush and easy rock to an obvious slabby rock face just left of the small pocket glacier on the east face.
targets.descent: Not known in detail; parties would descend via the standard west-ridge/southwest-slope route to Lake Elan and out over Headlee Pass.

targets.approach: From High Bridge, take the Park Creek trail up the Park Creek valley and climb to the snow line on the south side of the saddle between Goode and Storm King; the first party camped there. Gain the saddle, make one rappel onto the glacier on the north side, and descend it through crevasses and beneath an ice cliff to the foot of the roughly 3,000 ft rock rib that leads straight to the main (east) summit. Expect a bivy at the base of the rib.

wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead, hike the Stuart Lake Trail through the beaver meadows; at the first switchback past the meadows, beyond the Colchuck/Stuart Lake trail fork, leave the trail to the south on an obscure, unmaintained climbers' path, crossing Stuart Lake creek on logs, to reach the base of the northeast-facing couloir below Sherpa Peak. The path is unmaintained and can be hard to follow.
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.descent_text: Most parties reverse the couloir (downclimbing or rappelling the snow/ice) back to the approach path. An alternative used by some parties is to traverse to Sherpa Pass and downclimb from there to regain camp, avoiding a full re-descent of the steepest snow.
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.name: Northeast Couloir

wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.approach: Access is the same Esmeralda Basin/Longs Pass Trailhead used for the West Ridge: follow the Longs Pass Trail (#1229) over Longs Pass (~6,200 ft) and down to Ingalls Creek Trail, crossing Ingalls Creek and continuing on the climbers' boot path up into the Sherpa-Argonaut basin (see West Ridge approach for that shared section). From the basin, rather than aiming for the West Ridge notch, angle climber's-left (east), traversing a grassy slope and ascending a talus/scree gully to reach the prominent notch at roughly 8,000 ft, about 600 vertical feet below and east of the true summit. Gain the ridge crest about 100 ft above (east of) the notch via class 2 terrain. This line is longer and more circuitous through loose talus than the direct West Ridge approach, and picking the correct gully/notch is the main route-finding crux; a 50m rope is worth carrying from here since the route above uses fixed rappel slings at several obstacles.
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.descent_text: Most parties do not reverse the East Ridge; the accepted descent is to finish near the summit, traverse to the top of the West Ridge, and go down using the West Ridge's established rappel line (two single-rope rappels past the crux, a short scramble, another single, then a double-rope rappel to the west notch - see the West Ridge descent for full detail) before dropping back to the basin and Ingalls Creek. Some parties do reverse the East Ridge directly, especially when combining the climb with the nearby Balanced Rock feature: this involves downclimbing/rappelling a vertical chimney using chained-together fixed rappel slings, then a rappel down a steep gully to an exposed slab, then another rappel after crossing the slab, finishing with class 3 downclimbing to the 8,000-ft notch. Expect roughly 2-4 short single-rope rappels off existing (sometimes weathered) fixed slings and chains rather than full ropelength raps; a 50m rope was reported as sufficient. Back up any suspect fixed anchors with your own gear. From the notch/basin, reverse the approach: descend to Ingalls Creek Trail, cross the creek, and climb back over Longs Pass to the trailhead.
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.name: East Ridge

wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge.approach: The North Ridge is most commonly approached from the north via the Stuart Lake Trailhead (reached by Icicle Creek Road/Eightmile Creek Road out of Leavenworth). Follow the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599) along Mountaineer Creek roughly 3.5-4 miles, climbing gently through forest. Before reaching Stuart/Colchuck Lake, leave the maintained trail, cross Mountaineer Creek, and pick up a boot path/cairned route that climbs talus benches on the slope west of the creek, staying a couple hundred feet above the trees before dropping back toward the creek, aiming for the Argonaut-Sherpa basin. Around 5,800 ft, the route steepens into sustained loose talus leading up to the base of the North Ridge proper (~7,000 ft), a roughly 1,500-ft-tall rock feature capped by the 8,630-ft summit. At the base, contour and work climber's-right to a lower notch, where easy slabs can be scrambled before roping up. (A southern approach via Longs Pass and Ingalls Creek to Mountaineer Creek is also possible but is a longer, less direct line to this specific route.) Water is available at Mountaineer Creek but is limited higher on the talus approach - carry enough for the day. The talus benches and loose approach gully
wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge.descent_text: Descent is not a reversal of the North Ridge and is considered the trickiest part of the route. From the summit, downclimb/scramble a short distance to an established rappel station just west of the true summit - the top anchor of the standard West Ridge route - and make a short rappel (roughly 25-30 ft/one short pitch) down into a gully southwest of the summit. A second, shorter rappel (about 20 ft, off a slung boulder) follows; this one is optional and can be downclimbed at low 5th class by confident parties. Some parties describe this stage as two ~25m rappels rather than two short single-pitch raps, so treat the exact length as variable and carry a 50-60m rope to cover either version. Below the rappels, the terrain eases from sustained class 3 (roughly the first 500 ft) to class 2; continue southeast across loose rocky ribs and gullies, staying low to avoid cliff bands, toward the Sherpa-Argonaut saddle. The final ~1,000 ft down to treeline from the saddle is the descent's crux - loose rock only barely held in place by dirt and sand - so move carefully and stay alert for parties below. From the basin, either retrace the approach out via Mountaineer Creek and the Stuart Lake Tra
wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge.name: North Ridge

wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge.approach: From the Esmeralda Basin/Longs Pass Trailhead (end of Teanaway River Road/FS-9737, ~4,300 ft), take the Longs Pass Trail (#1229) roughly 2.3 miles and about 2,300 ft of gain to Longs Pass (~6,200 ft), a broad open saddle. From the pass, drop steeply down the north side (a boot path, with snow fingers usable for glissading in early season) about 1,300-1,400 ft to the Ingalls Creek drainage (~4,800 ft). Ford or rock-hop Ingalls Creek (can run high with early-season snowmelt) and pick up the Ingalls Creek Trail, following it right (east) about a half to full mile to the Beverly-Turnpike Trail junction. Leave the maintained trail here for a boot/climbers' path (sometimes called the "tapeworm trail") that switchbacks up through timber and brush before opening into meadow beneath Sherpa and Argonaut Peaks. Gain the rounded rib dividing the Cascadian Couloir drainage from the basin under Sherpa, then contour around 5,800 ft into the snow-holding basin below the West Ridge; kick steps up final snow/talus slopes to a common bivy/base-camp shelf around 7,400 ft (a flat table-rock area) or continue straight to the ridge base. Total gain from the car to the base of technical climbing runs roug
wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge.descent_text: The standard descent reverses the West Ridge using a sequence of rappels rather than downclimbing the whole route. From the summit area, two single-rope rappels lead down past the crux (5.4-5.6) pitch to a short 3rd-class scramble; this is followed by another single-rope rappel and then a longer double-rope rappel (two ropes joined, or a single 60m doubled) that returns you to the west notch below the technical climbing. Anchors are a mix of fixed slings around horns and flakes; most are solid (slings around big, well-set flakes/horns), but at least one reported station was backed by a sketchy bundle of slings wrapped around a few small loose rocks next to the actual load-bearing horn - inspect and back up questionable tat with your own gear. Some parties skip the last downclimb and instead rappel directly down the loose, dirty gully from the notch. Bring a 60m rope (or two ropes for the double-rope stretch) and extra slings/cord to replace weathered anchors. From the notch, descend scree/talus and boot path back into the basin (glissading is possible on lingering snow) to camp, then reverse the approach over Longs Pass to the trailhead. wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge.name: West Ridge

wa_accidental_discharge_east_face.approach: One approach is from the Downey Creek Trailhead (off Suiattle River Road) via the southern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse — a rugged, largely off-trail alpine route over Itswoot Ridge/Cub Lake and Bachelor Creek involving glacier travel and significant bushwhacking. Climbers typically budget a full day (or two) of approach before reaching South Peak. That way arrives on the Chickamin Glacier on the west side of the crest, while this route starts out of the moat of the Blue Glacier on the east side; the approach from the east up Agnes Creek puts you on that side directly. Either way this is an experienced-mountaineers-only objective, not a roadside crag.
wa_accidental_discharge_east_face.descent_text: Rappel off the summit by the same line as the peak's other routes: about 35 m north, then a second rappel east onto the Blue Glacier. The last rappel can hang free over the moat at the foot of the face, so land beyond the lip and carry cord to build or back up anchors rather than relying on fixed gear. Do not plan on reversing the loose line of ascent.
wa_accidental_discharge_east_face.name: Accidental Discharge (East Face)

wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.approach: From Highway 530 in Darrington, go south on Madison Avenue to the T, turn right on Darrington Street and follow it as it becomes Squire Creek Road (FS 2040) to the washout that blocks it. Walk or bike the old roadbed past the landslide crossing to the Squire Creek Trail #654 sign, then continue 8–10 minutes to two cut logs on either side of the track, with old logging cable low and just right of it. A few steps past the logs, turn right on a well-beaten boot track down to Squire Creek and ford it where it is shallowest — hard in early season or after storms. Across the creek, follow a climbers' track right (downstream); it soon turns uphill, crosses a tributary (also hard early in the season), climbs through old-growth forest and drops left into two gullies, which it follows up. The top of the second gully is steep and dirty and opens onto a grassy saddle with good bivy sites, near the start of Concerto. Allow about 3 hours from the car. This turn-off comes before the one for Waterfall Basin, which is farther along at a wide streambed of white boulders.
wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.descent_text: Rappel the line of ascent on fixed chain/bolt anchors; parties typically rappel to the Pitch 13 chain anchor near the summit before continuing down.
wa_concerto_in_c_for_drill_and_hammer.name: Concerto in C for Drill and Hammer

wa_east_ridge_3.approach: Start from the Cedar Creek trailhead near Mazama -- a different trailhead than the Silver Star Creek/Highway 20 pullout used for the Glacier and NE Ridge routes -- and gain the ridge near the confluence of Cedar and Early Winters Creeks, then follow the crest north and west for roughly 3.5 miles to the summit.
wa_east_ridge_3.descent_text: From the summit, rope down or downclimb a short distance to gain the Silver Star Glacier, then descend the glacier west/northwest toward Burgundy Col. From the col, climb/hike up and over to the Burgundy Col climbers' trail, which drops back to Highway 20 near milepost 166 (roughly 4 miles from Washington Pass) — several miles of highway from the Cedar Creek Trailhead used for the approach. Carry glacier travel gear (and an ice axe/crampons in early season) for this descent, since it crosses real crevassed glacier terrain, not just snow slopes.
wa_east_ridge_3.name: East Ridge

wa_primal_scream.approach: From the grassy saddle bivy, cross class 4 ramps to a shallow dihedral with a small tree, then continue to a dirt ledge at the base of a short wall marking the start.
wa_primal_scream.descent_text: Rappel the line of ascent using the 2023-installed modern bolted anchors; the upper three pitches share anchors with Concerto in C for Drill and Hammer.
wa_primal_scream.name: Primal Scream

wa_silver_star_glacier.approach: Park at the broad pullout/overlook on SR-20 near milepost 165–166 (about 4 miles east of Washington Pass), where a sign points toward Silver Star Mountain. From the pullout, drop down the embankment roughly 150–200 ft to Early Winters Creek and cross on a log (logjams shift year to year — scout up- and downstream for the best crossing, and be ready to ford in high water/early season, when the creek runs cold and fast with snowmelt). On the far bank, pick up the unofficial but well-defined climber's trail that climbs the timbered rib on the west (left) side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. From here the trail climbs relentlessly and steeply through forest and brush for roughly 2,500–3,000 ft with almost no switchbacks and only fleeting creek-side water access early on — treat the crossing at Early Winters Creek as your last reliable water until camp. At around 6,000–6,400 ft the grade eases at 'the Bench,' an open larch-and-heather shelf with several established campsites and usually a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby; this is the standard overnight camp for a two-day trip and a natural break point/turnaround check for day-trippers. Above the bench, continue up open subalpine terr
wa_silver_star_glacier.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent route. From the summit, downclimb the short class 3–4 rock (the same easy, somewhat exposed ledge system used on the way up) back to the col between the east and west summits; several trip reports and topo photos document a natural/slung rappel anchor near the true summit that parties use to bypass the most exposed section of this downclimb — a single rappel with one 50 m rope (or a 60 m rope doubled) is enough to get below the crux and onto easier ground, though plenty of parties simply downclimb the whole way and skip it entirely, so treat this as an optional, not mandatory, rappel with a natural anchor (sling on a horn/block), not bolts. From the base of the summit scramble, work back down onto the Silver Star Glacier and re-descend it, wrapping below the rock slabs of Burgundy Spire; note that this traverse dips below the elevation of Burgundy Col, so you must reclimb a couple hundred feet of steep snow from the low point back up to the col — a sting in the tail that catches parties expecting a pure descent. From Burgundy Col, downclimb the steep snow and loose, unstable 'kitty litter' rock/gully back toward the bench; this section is notoriously
wa_silver_star_glacier.name: Silver Star Glacier

wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.approach: Park in the Alpental lot at the end of Alpental Rd (NW Forest Pass required at the trailhead kiosk). Walk toward the signed Snow Lake trailhead, but instead of taking that trail, look for an unsigned boot path/old roadbed about 50 ft downhill (south) of the Snow Lake trailhead sign, dropping into a band of slide alder — this is the shared start for both Guye Peak and Snoqualmie Mountain. The path immediately steepens and follows a creek drainage (Source Creek) up through roots, talus, and brush; it is a climbers' path only, not a maintained trail, and can be hard to follow in the alder in early season or after blowdown. At roughly 1 mile / ~1,000 ft gain, a junction splits: the right fork climbs to Guye Peak and Cave Ridge proper, while the main Snoqualmie route continues left/straight. About a third of a mile past that junction the path fords the creek near a 50-ft waterfall (the main water source on route — treat before drinking); a quarter mile beyond the crossing it breaks out of the trees onto the open west-facing gully/slope below Cave Ridge and switchbacks steeply up this slope for roughly the final mile to the summit ridge and the true summit at 6,278 ft. Expect loose scree
wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.descent_text: This is a walk-off, not a rappel route — descend by reversing the ascent gully/climbers' path back down through Cave Ridge's west slope, past the waterfall creek crossing and the Guye Peak junction, to the Alpental lot. No rappelling or fixed anchors are involved (rappels = 0). The descent is the crux for many parties: the scree/dirt path is looser and harder to control on the way down than it looks going up, and the upper gully holds snow into summer, so in spring conditions a glissade down the snow-filled chute is a common (faster) alternative to the dry boot path — carry an ice axe and know self-arrest if attempting it, since the gully funnels into trees and rock lower down. In winter and spring this same gully is recognized avalanche terrain (a frequent subject of NWAC-relevant trip reports and Mountaineers winter scramble/ski trip logs), so check avalanche conditions and be prepared to bail to Cave Ridge rather than push through unstable snow. Watch footing carefully near the top where the ridge narrows and exposure increases just below the summit.
wa_snoqualmie_mountain_standard_route.name: Standard Route (Southwest Slopes)

wa_south_ridge.approach: The genuine standard approach is from the Downey Creek Trailhead (off Suiattle River Road) via the southern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse — a rugged, largely off-trail alpine route up Bachelor Creek past Cub Lake and over Itswoot Ridge, involving glacier travel and significant bushwhacking. Climbers typically budget a full day (or two) of approach before reaching the base of South Peak's granite faces; this is an experienced-mountaineers-only objective, not a roadside crag.
wa_south_ridge.descent_text: Do not reverse the ridge. Rappel about 35 m north off the summit, then make a second rappel east onto the Blue Glacier; a moat usually separates rock from ice at the bottom. Carry two 60 m ropes — joined, they give rappels of up to a full 60 m, enough to reach past the lip of the moat — and cord to leave an anchor.
wa_south_ridge.name: South Ridge

wa_sperry_peak_standard.approach: From the Sunrise Mine Trailhead (2,350 ft, end of FS Road 4065), follow the Sunrise Mine Trail (#707) into the Morning Star NRCA. About 0.5 mile in, the trail makes a tricky crossing of the South Fork Stillaguamish River — no bridge, sometimes aided by a small-diameter log and a hand rope; this ford can be genuinely difficult and dangerous after heavy rain or early-season snowmelt. Beyond the crossing the trail climbs gradually through forest for roughly a mile to Wirtz Basin, where the terrain opens up and turns rockier. From the basin the trail steepens sharply into a narrow, loose rock chute switchbacking up to Headlee Pass (4,720 ft, about 2.7 miles from the trailhead) — this chute is notorious for rockfall dislodged by parties above and is also an avalanche path in shoulder-season/spring snow conditions, so groups should spread out and move through it deliberately. From Headlee Pass the trail contours around Sperry's south/east flank and drops slightly into the upper Vesper Creek basin to Vesper Lake (Lake Elan, roughly 3 miles in). Leave the maintained trail at the lake's outlet, follow its east shore, then climb open, welcoming slopes to the saddle/notch between Vesper and S
wa_sperry_peak_standard.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the loose, brushy west ridge/west slope scramble back to Sperry Saddle, then drop to the Vesper Lake outlet and rejoin the maintained Sunrise Mine Trail. Route-finding on the upper scramble is the main hazard on the way down — the easiest line up is not obvious from above, and it's easy to end up descending a different, steeper gully than the one you climbed, so note landmarks (the climber's-right ramp and the cairned dirt path into the trees) on the way up and look for them again on the way down. From the lake, retrace the trail back through Headlee Pass and down its rockfall-prone switchback chute (loose underfoot, stay alert for rock knocked loose by other parties), through Wirtz Basin, back across the South Fork Stillaguamish ford, and out to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble route with no rappelling involved anywhere on the standard line.
wa_sperry_peak_standard.name: Standard Scramble

wa_sperry_peak_upper_south_ridge.approach: Approach to Headlee Pass as for the standard route (see that route's approach). Cross the talus toward Vesper/Elan Lake, then take the first ramp heading up and to the right to reach the base of the South Ridge.
wa_sperry_peak_upper_south_ridge.descent_text: From the summit, follow the standard Class 3 route down to the west to the pass between Vesper and Sperry, then head south back over Headlee Pass and down to the car - do not try to reverse the South Ridge itself.
wa_sperry_peak_upper_south_ridge.name: Upper South Ridge

wa_storm_king_southwest_scramble.approach: Storm King sits at the head of Thunder Creek in the North Cascades and is one of the range's most remote 'Bulger/Top 100' summits — a three-day car-to-car trip is the norm, and three separate trailhead approaches converge on the same high basin below Mount Goode's south side. The most common line is the Thunder Creek approach: from the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead on SR-20, follow the Thunder Creek Trail (an easy, mostly-forested stock/hiker trail) about 13 miles with only ~600 ft of gain to the McAllister Creek confluence — McAllister Camp (~mile 6) is a common night-one camp. Continue past Junction Camp (~mile 9.5) and Skagit Queen Camp (~mile 13.5) to Thunder Basin Camp (~mile 16.5), then pick up the signed Park Creek Pass Trail junction a couple miles beyond and follow it up through meadows to Park Creek Pass. Two alternate approaches reach the same basin: a steeper, more direct line over McAlester Pass and down Rainbow Creek from SR-20 (camp at Rainbow Lake, ~9 mi and 2,700 ft of gain), or a southern approach via boat/shuttle to Stehekin and High Bridge Camp, then up the Park Creek Trail to Park Creek Pass from the south. wa_storm_king_southwest_scramble.descent_text: Descent reverses the ascent line. From the notch/crack area just below the true summit, most parties downclimb the ~15-ft crux crack and the exposed Class 4 ledge just below it. Some instead rappel off the fixed slings (in-situ tat/webbing — inspect it and back it up before committing) back to the ledge on the north side; even with a 60 m rope, expect to downclimb some Class 3 terrain. From the ledge, cross back through the right-most notch and descend the loose talus and scree slope to the cirque. From the base of the talus, traverse back to the basin below Goode and descend the cairned climbers' path and the burned ridge to the Park Creek trail just past the big washout, then continue via whichever of the three approach trails (Thunder Creek, McAlester Pass/Rainbow Creek, or Park Creek/Stehekin) matches your itinerary. Loose rock is the dominant descent hazard from the summit all the way down through the talus — keep helmets on and parties tight until well below the scree.
wa_storm_king_southwest_scramble.name: Southwest Scramble

wa_summit_chief_mountain_north_face.approach: Approach from the Middle Fork Snoqualmie valley (North Bend side): drive the Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road (NF-56) to its plowed/drivable end, then bike or hike the remaining distance (about 1 mile in the FA party's case) into the valley. Continue on foot through snowy forest along the valley trail, crossing multiple braids of the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River (the crux of the approach in high water), then climb to a camp below the north face. The FA party's full approach from vehicle to camp took about 6.5 hours.
wa_summit_chief_mountain_north_face.descent_text: From the summit area, downclimb neve on the southwest aspect to the top of a snow gully, then make two 30m rappels down the gully to regain lower-angle terrain and return toward the approach basin/camp.
wa_summit_chief_mountain_north_face.name: North Face

wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.approach: Start at the Pete Lake Trailhead (~2,840 ft) at the end of Cooper Lake Road (Forest Road 46) off the Salmon La Sac Road. Follow the Pete Lake Trail (#1323) roughly 4.5 miles of gentle, mostly flat forest walking along the Cooper River to Pete Lake. From Pete Lake, continue up the Lemah Creek/Lemah Meadows drainage (watch for windfall and thick vine maple in the meadow bypass) to join the Pacific Crest Trail; turn right (north) and climb the PCT's long switchback section roughly 4-4.5 more miles to Lower and Upper Vista Lake (~5,500-5,600 ft) — camp is commonly made here, making this a two-day approach of about 10 miles and 2,800 ft to reach the alpine basin. This is also the last reliable water before the high basin — carry extra, as the route above is reported bone-dry until you're back near Vista Lakes. From Vista Lakes, leave the PCT and traverse cross-country north along Vista Ridge toward Summit Chief Pass, crossing a convoluted series of sandstone/siltstone slabs cut by numerous slots and gullies; stay left (west) of Summit Chief Lake and minimize elevation loss while rounding into the southeast basin below the peak. wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb — no rappelling is involved on the standard South Route. Reverse the ascent line exactly: downclimb the loose, exposed southwest gully and its outward-dipping slab back to the ~7,200 ft notch, taking care with the loose rock and steep dirt in the upper 500 feet (this section has real rockfall potential for parties below). Continue down through the talus and hardpan to the 6,300 ft basin (recover any stashed gear here), then retrace the slab traverses back onto Vista Ridge and down to Vista Lakes/the PCT. From Vista Lakes, follow the PCT switchbacks back down to Lemah Meadows and the Pete Lake Trail, then out to the Pete Lake Trailhead. Some parties vary the return by continuing along the PCT to Waptus Lake and crossing Waptus Pass back to the Pete Lake trailhead as an alternate loop. The round trip runs roughly 25 miles car to car, so most parties treat this as an overnight with a basin or Vista Lakes camp rather than a single push.
wa_summit_chief_mountain_south_route.name: South Route
